microwave-001.question: For a hollow rectangular metal waveguide with inside dimensions a × b (a > b), which is the fundamental mode, the one that propagates from the lowest frequency?
microwave-001.explanation: The fundamental mode of a rectangular waveguide is TE10. Its electric field points only perpendicular to the broad walls (the sides of width a) and forms a single half-wavelength peak across the a dimension. Its cutoff frequency is fc = c/(2a), the lowest of all modes. The TEM mode, in which both the electric and magnetic fields are perpendicular to the direction of propagation, cannot exist without two conductors, as in a coaxial line, so it does not propagate in a hollow waveguide with a single conductor. TM11 is the lowest TM mode, but its cutoff frequency is c/2·√((1/a)² + (1/b)²), which is always higher than that of TE10.

microwave-002.question: For an air-filled rectangular waveguide with inside dimensions a = 25 mm and b = 12.5 mm, what is the cutoff frequency of the TE10 mode? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
choices: There is no cutoff frequency; any frequency propagates
microwave-002.explanation: The TE10 cutoff is the frequency at which the broad dimension a is exactly half a wavelength: fc = c/(2a) = 3×10⁸/(2 × 0.025) = 6×10⁹ Hz, or 6 GHz. 12 GHz uses the narrow dimension b, c/(2b); with these dimensions it is the cutoff of the TE01 mode (and of the TE20 mode, with two peaks across a). Every waveguide mode has a cutoff frequency, and frequencies below it do not propagate. Only the TEM (or quasi-TEM) mode of two-conductor lines such as coaxial lines and microstrip has no cutoff.

microwave-003.question: What happens when a signal below the TE10 cutoff frequency is fed into a rectangular waveguide?
choices: It still propagates in the TE10 mode, but more slowly than the speed of light
It converts to the TEM mode and propagates without loss
It does not propagate in the guide, and the field decays exponentially from the entrance (an evanescent wave)
microwave-003.explanation: Below the cutoff frequency, the waveguide's propagation constant changes from purely imaginary to real, and the wave does not travel but weakens exponentially with distance. This is called an evanescent wave (an attenuating mode); it carries no power, and the signal is almost entirely reflected at the entrance. This property is used in cutoff attenuators, which give a large attenuation over a set length, and in the honeycomb panels (plates of small holes) used as ventilation openings in electromagnetic shields. "It propagates but more slowly" refers to the group velocity above cutoff; below cutoff, the wave itself does not propagate. A hollow waveguide has no TEM mode, so the signal cannot convert to TEM either.

microwave-004.question: A rectangular waveguide whose broad dimension a is exactly twice its narrow dimension b (a = 2b) is to be used with only the TE10 mode propagating (single-mode operation). With fc the TE10 cutoff frequency, what is the usable frequency range?
microwave-004.explanation: The TE10 cutoff is fc = c/(2a). The next lowest modes are TE20, with two peaks across a (cutoff c/a = 2fc), and TE01, with one peak across b (cutoff c/(2b)); with a = 2b both are at 2fc. So only TE10 propagates from fc to 2fc. Anywhere above fc is not acceptable: above 2fc higher-order modes also propagate, and mode conversion at discontinuities disturbs the response. Below fc, no mode propagates at all. In practice, waveguides are generally used from about 1.25fc to 1.9fc to avoid the loss and dispersion near cutoff.

microwave-005.question: A 12.5 GHz signal travels in the TE10 mode in an air-filled rectangular waveguide whose broad inside dimension is a = 20 mm. Which is closest to the guide wavelength? Take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s and the guide wavelength as λg = λ0/√(1 − (fc/f)²), where λ0 is the free-space wavelength.
microwave-005.explanation: The TE10 cutoff is fc = c/(2a) = 3×10⁸/0.04 = 7.5 GHz, and the free-space wavelength is λ0 = c/f = 3×10⁸/(12.5×10⁹) = 24 mm. With fc/f = 0.6, √(1 − 0.36) = 0.8, so λg = 24/0.8 = 30 mm. 24 mm is the free-space wavelength itself, overlooking that the wavelength inside a waveguide is longer than in free space. 19.2 mm multiplies by 0.8 instead of dividing. The wavelength is longer in the guide because the wave travels by bouncing obliquely off the walls, so its phase advances more slowly as seen along the axis.

microwave-006.question: For a wave above cutoff traveling in an air-filled waveguide, which correctly describes the phase velocity vp and group velocity vg (c is the speed of light)?
choices: Both vp and vg equal c
vp is less than c, and vg is greater than c
vp is greater than c, vg is less than c, and vp·vg = c²
microwave-006.explanation: A wave in a waveguide can be viewed as a superposition of plane waves bouncing obliquely off the walls. The phase pattern seen along the axis moves faster than c, so vp = c/√(1 − (fc/f)²) > c. The speed at which energy and information travel along the axis is the group velocity, vg = c·√(1 − (fc/f)²) < c. Multiplying the two gives vp·vg = c². A phase velocity above c does not violate relativity, because information is carried at the group velocity. Both vp and vg equal c on a TEM-mode line such as an air-filled coaxial line. The option with the inequalities reversed mistakes which velocity carries the information.

microwave-007.question: Which is closest to the TE101 resonant frequency of an air-filled rectangular cavity resonator with inside dimensions a = 30 mm and d = 30 mm (the height b is smaller than a)? Use f = (c/2)√((1/a)² + (1/d)²) and take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
microwave-007.explanation: Substituting into the formula, f = (3×10⁸/2) × √((1/0.03)² + (1/0.03)²) = 1.5×10⁸ × 33.3 × √2 ≈ 7.07×10⁹ Hz, or about 7.1 GHz. The TE101 mode corresponds to a TE10 waveguide closed at both ends with metal so that half a guide wavelength fits in the length d. About 5.0 GHz drops the d term, giving c/(2a), the waveguide's cutoff frequency. About 10 GHz simply adds the terms, (c/2)(1/a + 1/d), where they should be added inside the square root. Cavity resonators give far higher Q than LC circuits, so they are used for microwave frequency standards, filters and wavemeters.

microwave-008.question: Which statement about the unloaded Q of a metal cavity resonator (the Q excluding loss from coupling to external circuits) is correct?
choices: It is set mainly by the loss from skin currents flowing in the conductor walls, and the higher the wall conductivity, the higher it is
The stronger the coupling to external circuits, the higher it becomes
It is set mainly by the loss from electromagnetic waves radiated out of the cavity
microwave-008.explanation: A closed metal cavity does not radiate, and when it is air-filled almost all of its loss is Joule loss from skin currents in the walls. The surface resistance Rs = √(πfμρ) is proportional to the square root of the resistivity ρ, so walls of lower resistivity, such as silver plating, lose less and give a higher Q. Unloaded Qs of several thousand to tens of thousands are obtained at microwave frequencies. Stronger coupling to external circuits draws more power out, which lowers the loaded Q (1/QL = 1/Q0 + 1/Qext) but leaves the unloaded Q unchanged. Radiation dominates in open structures such as antennas, not in closed cavities. If the cavity is filled with a dielectric, the dielectric loss (tan δ) is added as well.

microwave-009.question: For an air-filled coaxial line with outer-conductor inner diameter D = 7 mm and inner-conductor outer diameter d = 3 mm, which is closest to the frequency at which the first higher-order mode, TE11, begins to propagate (its cutoff frequency)? Use fc ≈ c/(π(D + d)/2) and take the speed of light as 3×10⁸ m/s.
microwave-009.explanation: The TE11 cutoff wavelength is roughly equal to the mean circumference of the inner and outer conductors, π(D + d)/2. π × (7 + 3)/2 mm ≈ 15.7 mm, so fc ≈ 3×10⁸/0.0157 ≈ 1.9×10¹⁰ Hz, about 19 GHz (the exact value from the Bessel-function solution is about 19.5 GHz; the approximation is off by a few percent). About 9.5 GHz forgets the 1/2 and uses π(D + d) as the wavelength, and about 43 GHz uses the outer diameter D directly as the wavelength. The fundamental TEM mode of a coaxial line has no cutoff, but once TE11 starts to propagate the line is no longer single-mode. Connectors and cables for higher frequencies are thinner in order to keep this cutoff above the operating frequency.

microwave-010.question: What is the main purpose of placing an isolator between the output of a microwave oscillator or power amplifier and its load (such as an antenna)?
choices: To absorb waves reflected back from the load, preventing frequency changes in or damage to the oscillator or amplifier
To split the signal equally in power between two outputs
To attenuate harmonics and clean up the output spectrum
microwave-010.explanation: An isolator is a nonreciprocal device that passes signals in the forward direction with little loss (insertion loss) and gives large attenuation (isolation) in the reverse direction. It uses a ferrite under a DC magnetic field, whose effect on electromagnetic waves depends on the direction of travel. By absorbing waves reflected by a load mismatch, it prevents the oscillator frequency from being pulled by changes in the load (frequency pulling) and protects the amplifier output from damage by reflections. Splitting power in two is the job of power dividers such as the Wilkinson divider, and removing harmonics is the job of a low-pass filter. An isolator selects the direction of travel, not the frequency.

microwave-011.question: An oscillator with a +20 dBm output is connected to an isolator with 0.5 dB forward insertion loss and 20 dB reverse isolation, followed by a load with 10 dB return loss. Which is closest to the power reflected by the load that returns to the oscillator (ignore cable loss and other reflections)?
microwave-011.explanation: The power reaching the load is 20 − 0.5 = 19.5 dBm, and with a 10 dB return loss the reflected power is 19.5 − 10 = 9.5 dBm. This reflected wave passes back through the isolator in the reverse direction and is attenuated by 20 dB, so the power returning to the oscillator is 9.5 − 20 = −10.5 dBm. +9.5 dBm forgets the isolator's reverse attenuation; without the isolator, about this much power would come back. −0.5 dBm forgets to subtract the load's return loss and treats the reflection as total. A helpful way to see the isolator's effect is that the load's return loss plus the isolation becomes the effective return loss seen by the oscillator (here about 30 dB).

microwave-012.question: You want to measure the average power of a modulated signal with a high peak-to-average power ratio, such as OFDM, accurately. Which power sensor is most suitable?
choices: A diode-detector sensor used at large inputs beyond its square-law region
Reading the peak voltage Vp on an oscilloscope and computing Vp²/R
microwave-012.explanation: Thermal sensors, such as thermocouple and thermistor types, measure the temperature rise from the absorbed RF power, so they indicate the true average power regardless of waveform or modulation. Diode-detector sensors are sensitive and fast, but their output is proportional to power only in the square-law region at small inputs (roughly −20 dBm and below, depending on the sensor). Beyond that, the reading is pulled toward the envelope peaks, causing large errors with modulated signals. Computing Vp²/R from the peak voltage gives twice the correct average power Vp²/(2R) even for a sine wave, and is even further off for modulated signals with large peaks. The drawbacks of thermal sensors are their slow response and low sensitivity.

microwave-013.question: A diode detector operating in its square-law region gives a DC output of 1 mV for a −30 dBm input. Which is closest to the output voltage when the input is raised to −20 dBm (assume it stays in the square-law region)?
microwave-013.explanation: In the square-law region, the diode's output voltage is proportional to the square of the input RF voltage, that is, to the input power. Going from −30 dBm to −20 dBm increases the power tenfold, so the output also rises tenfold, to 10 mV. About 3.2 mV (√10 times) wrongly assumes the output is proportional to the input voltage; that is the behavior in the linear (peak) detection region at large inputs. 100 mV squares the power ratio again. Because of this property, a diode detector in its square-law region can be used as a power meter, but at large inputs it moves into the linear detection region, so sensors are specified with a usable power range.

microwave-014.question: Which is the correct reason PIN diodes can be used as microwave switches and variable attenuators?
choices: Under reverse bias their resistance drops, so they pass RF signals
The lifetime of the carriers stored in the i-region is much longer than the RF period, so the diode does not rectify the RF and acts as a resistance set by the DC bias current
When the RF signal amplitude is smaller than the forward voltage (about 0.7 V), the diode automatically stops conducting
microwave-014.explanation: When a forward DC current flows through a PIN diode, carriers injected into the i-region lower its resistance, and the value is set by the bias current. If the carrier lifetime (from several hundred ns to a few µs) is much longer than the RF period, the carriers in the i-region hardly change during one RF cycle, so the diode does not rectify and behaves simply as a resistance. Under reverse bias, the i-region is depleted and acts as a small capacitance that blocks the signal. The option saying resistance drops under reverse bias has it backward. Not conducting at small amplitudes is the small-signal view of an ordinary PN junction diode; a PIN diode switch has its state set by the bias, so it does not depend on the signal amplitude.

microwave-015.question: A switch consists of a single PIN diode placed in series in a 50 Ω line. If the diode can be treated as a 0.1 pF capacitance under reverse bias (off), which is closest to the isolation (the attenuation in |S21|) at 10 GHz? For a series impedance Z, take |S21| = |2Z0/(2Z0 + Z)|.
microwave-015.explanation: The reactance of 0.1 pF is X = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × 10¹⁰ × 10⁻¹³) ≈ 159 Ω. With Z = −j159 Ω, |S21| = 100/|100 − j159| = 100/√(100² + 159²) ≈ 100/188 ≈ 0.53, so the isolation is about 5.5 dB. About 8.3 dB treats Z as a pure resistance, 100/(100 + 159); a reactance must be combined as the square root of the sum of squares. About 20 dB forgets the 2π, taking the reactance as 1/(fC) = 1000 Ω. Even 0.1 pF cannot block 10 GHz well enough, so in practice shunt diodes are combined with the series one, or the capacitance is parallel-resonated with an inductor.
